claim: When you create a hosted zone, Route 53 creates a name server (NS) record and a start of authority (SOA) record for it. The NS record lists the four name servers that you give to your registrar or DNS service so that DNS queries reach Route 53 name servers.
question: Which records does Route 53 create when you create a hosted zone, and what does the NS record hold?

values.display: a name server (NS) record and a start of authority (SOA) record
lists the four name servers

evidence.quote: When you create a hosted zone, Amazon Route 53 creates a name server (NS) record and a start of authority (SOA) record for the zone. The NS record lists the four name servers that you give to your registrar or your DNS service so that DNS queries reach Route 53 name servers.

claim: You can create more than one hosted zone with the same name and add different records to each. Route 53 gives each of them its own four name servers.
question: Can you create more than one Route 53 hosted zone with the same name?

values.display: more than one hosted zone with the same name
the name servers differ for each one

evidence.quote: You can create more than one hosted zone with the same name and add different records to each. Route 53 assigns four name servers to every hosted zone, and the name servers differ for each one.

claim: Route 53 never returns values for records in other hosted zones that have the same name. Only the zone whose name servers your registrar lists answers queries.
question: If two hosted zones have the same name, which one answers queries for the domain?

values.display: never returns values for records in other hosted zones
use the Route 53 name servers for the correct hosted zone

qualifiers.scope: public hosted zones with the same name

evidence.quote: When you update your registrar's name server records, be careful to use the Route 53 name servers for the correct hosted zone—the one that has the records you want Route 53 to use when responding to queries for your domain. Route 53 never returns values for records in other hosted zones that have the same name.

claim: By default, Route 53 assigns a unique set of four name servers, called a delegation set, to each hosted zone that you create.
question: By default, how many name servers does a new hosted zone get, and are they shared with other zones?

values.display: a unique set of four name servers
called a delegation set

evidence.quote: By default, Route 53 assigns a unique set of four name servers (called a delegation set) to each hosted zone that you create.

claim: You create a reusable delegation set with the API, because it is not available in the Route 53 console. It lets you give your registrar the same four name servers for all the domains you move to Route 53, which simplifies DNS migration.
question: Why use a reusable delegation set, and can you create one in the console?

values.display: aren't available in the Route 53 console
simpler to migrate DNS service to Route 53
same four name servers for all the domains

evidence.quote: (Reusable delegation sets aren't available in the Route 53 console.)
Reusable delegation sets make it simpler to migrate DNS service to Route 53.
You can tell your registrar to use the same four name servers for all the domains that you want Route 53 to serve.

claim: To migrate a hosted zone to another AWS account, you create the new hosted zone in the account that you migrate to, and then migrate the records from the old hosted zone to the new one.
question: How do you migrate a Route 53 hosted zone to a different AWS account?

values.display: Create the new hosted zone in the account
migrate records from an AWS account to another

evidence.quote: Create the new hosted zone in the account you want to migrate the hosted zone to.
You can migrate records from an AWS account to another by using the console or the AWS CLI.

claim: For a zone with a large number of records, you can export the records to a file, edit the file, and use it to create the records in the new hosted zone.
question: How can you move a large number of records to a new hosted zone?

values.display: export the records you want to migrate to a file
use the edited file to create records

evidence.quote: If your zone contains a large number of records, you can export the records you want to migrate to a file, edit the file, and then use the edited file to create records in the new hosted zone.

claim: When you edit the exported records for the new zone, put the alias records at the bottom of the file, because Route 53 must create the record that an alias record refers to before it can create the alias record.
question: Why must alias records be last when you import records into the new hosted zone?

values.display: Move the alias records to the bottom of the file
must create the record that an alias record refers to before

evidence.quote: Move the alias records to the bottom of the file. Route 53 must create the record that an alias record refers to before it can create the alias record.

claim: To migrate a Route 53 health check to a new account, you create new health checks in the new account with the same configuration as the existing ones.
question: Can health checks be moved to another account together with a hosted zone?

values.display: create new health checks in your new account
same configuration as your existing ones

evidence.quote: To migrate a Route 53 health check, you need to create new health checks in your new account with the same configuration as your existing ones.

claim: Route 53 does not currently support migrating the DNSSEC setting. Before the migration you disable DNSSEC validation by removing the DS record from the parent zone.
question: Can the DNSSEC setting of a hosted zone be migrated to another account?

values.display: does not currently support migrating the DNSSEC setting
removing the DS record from the parent zone

evidence.quote: Route 53 does not currently support migrating the DNSSEC setting. As such, you will need to disable DNSSEC validation performed against your domain prior to the migration by removing the DS record from the parent zone.

claim: Alias records route traffic to selected AWS resources, such as CloudFront distributions and S3 buckets, and from one record in a hosted zone to another record.
question: What is an alias record in Route 53 and what can it route traffic to?

values.display: route traffic to selected AWS resources
from one record in a hosted zone to another record

evidence.quote: Alias records let you route traffic to selected AWS resources, such as CloudFront distributions and Amazon S3 buckets. They also let you route traffic from one record in a hosted zone to another record.

claim: Unlike a CNAME record, you can create an alias record at the zone apex, the top node of a DNS namespace. For example.com, the zone apex is example.com.
question: Can you create an alias record at the zone apex, and what is the zone apex?

values.display: the top node of a DNS namespace
you can create an alias record
also known as the *zone apex*

qualifiers.scope: alias record at the zone apex

evidence.quote: Unlike a CNAME record, you can create an alias record at the top node of a DNS namespace, also known as the *zone apex*. For example, if you register the DNS name example.com, the zone apex is example.com.

claim: You cannot create a CNAME record that has the same name as the hosted zone (the zone apex). This is true for hosted zones for domain names and for hosted zones for subdomains.
question: Can you create a CNAME record at the zone apex?

values.display: You can't create a CNAME record
the same name as the hosted zone (the zone apex)

evidence.quote: You can't create a CNAME record that has the same name as the hosted zone (the zone apex). This is true both for hosted zones for domain names (example.com) and for hosted zones for subdomains (zenith.example.com).

claim: An alias record at the zone apex cannot redirect to a record in the same hosted zone that has the type CNAME. The alias record must have the same type as the record it routes to, and a CNAME at the zone apex is not supported.
question: What is the one exception to creating an alias record at the zone apex?

values.display: The one exception
must have the same type as the record you're routing traffic to

qualifiers.scope: alias record at the zone apex

evidence.quote: In most configurations, you can create an alias record that has the same name as the hosted zone (the zone apex). The one exception is when you want to redirect queries from the zone apex (such as example.com) to a record in the same hosted zone that has a type of CNAME (such as zenith.example.com). The alias record must have the same type as the record you're routing traffic to, and creating a CNAME record for the zone apex isn't supported even for an alias record.

claim: An alias record can only redirect queries to selected AWS resources, such as S3 buckets, CloudFront distributions or another record in the same hosted zone. A CNAME record, in contrast, can redirect to any DNS record.
question: Can an alias record redirect to any DNS name, like a CNAME record can?

values.display: can only redirect queries to selected AWS resources
A CNAME record can redirect DNS queries to any DNS record

evidence.quote: An alias record can only redirect queries to selected AWS resources, including but not limited to the following:
A CNAME record can redirect DNS queries to any DNS record.

claim: A CNAME record can redirect queries to a name outside your domain, and you do not need to use Route 53 as the DNS service for the domain that it redirects to.
question: Does a CNAME target have to be hosted in Route 53?

values.display: You don't need to use Route 53 as the DNS service

evidence.quote: You don't need to use Route 53 as the DNS service for the domain that you're redirecting queries to.

claim: You can create CNAME records only for subdomains. An alias record works for both the root domain and subdomains.
question: For which names can you create a CNAME record, and for which an alias record?

values.display: CNAME records only for subdomains
an alias record both for the root domain

evidence.quote: It's similar to a CNAME record, except you can create an alias record both for the root domain, such as example.com, and for subdomains, such as www.example.com. You can create CNAME records only for subdomains.

claim: Route 53 does not charge for alias queries to AWS resources. It does charge for CNAME queries.
question: Does Route 53 charge for alias queries and for CNAME queries?

values.display: doesn't charge for alias queries to AWS resources
Route 53 charges for CNAME queries

evidence.quote: Route 53 doesn't charge for alias queries to AWS resources.
Route 53 charges for CNAME queries.

claim: A CNAME that redirects to the name of another record in a Route 53 hosted zone is charged as two queries per DNS query. If it redirects to a record hosted with another DNS service, Route 53 charges for one query.
question: How many queries is a DNS query charged as when a CNAME redirects to another Route 53 record?

values.display: each DNS query is charged as two queries
Route 53 charges for one query

evidence.quote: If you create a CNAME record that redirects to the name of another record in a Route 53 hosted zone (the same hosted zone or another hosted zone), each DNS query is charged as two queries:
If the CNAME record redirects to the name of a record that is hosted with another DNS service, Route 53 charges for one query.

claim: Route 53 answers a query for an alias record only when the name and the type of the alias record match the name and type in the DNS query.
question: When does Route 53 respond to a DNS query for an alias record?

values.display: match the name and type in the DNS query
responds to a DNS query only when

evidence.quote: Route 53 responds to a DNS query only when the name of the alias record (such as acme.example.com) and the type of the alias record (such as A or AAAA) match the name and type in the DNS query.

claim: A CNAME record redirects DNS queries for a record name regardless of the record type in the query, such as A or AAAA.
question: Does a CNAME record depend on the record type in the DNS query?

values.display: regardless of the record type specified in the DNS query

evidence.quote: A CNAME record redirects DNS queries for a record name regardless of the record type specified in the DNS query, such as A or AAAA.

claim: When an alias record points to an AWS resource, Route 53 detects changes in the resource on its own. If the IP address of a load balancer changes, Route 53 starts answering with the new IP address.

starts responding to DNS queries with the new IP address

evidence.quote: When you use an alias record to route traffic to an AWS resource, Route 53 detects changes in the resource on its own.
If the IP address of the load balancer changes, Route 53 starts responding to DNS queries with the new IP address.

claim: If an alias record points to an AWS resource, you cannot set the TTL. Route 53 uses the default TTL for the resource.

evidence.quote: If an alias record points to an AWS resource, you can't set the time to live (TTL); Route 53 uses the default TTL for the resource.

qualifiers.scope: alias record to another record in the same hosted zone
